questions.question: Q: What was the patron-client system and why was it important?

points.text: A social network where patrons (wealthy elites) provided protection, financial help and political access to clients (lower-status Romans) in exchange for loyalty, votes and services. It was the glue of Roman society, linking all classes in mutual obligation.

questions.question: Q: How did the position of freedmen differ from that of slaves?

points.text: Freedmen (liberti) were former slaves granted freedom and citizenship. They could own property and run businesses, but they still owed obligations to their former master and carried the social stigma of their slave origins.
The absolute legal authority of the paterfamilias over his household — including his wife, children and slaves. In early Rome this included the right of life and death over family members.

questions.question: Q: How did the equestrian order differ from the senatorial class?

points.text: Equites (equestrians) were wealthy businessmen who could not hold the highest political offices, while senators were the political elite. Both were wealthy, but senators pursued political careers while equites focused on commerce.

questions.question: Q: How much social mobility was possible in Rome?

points.text: Limited but real: freedmen's children became full citizens, and talented individuals could rise through the patron-client system or military service. However, patrician birth remained the greatest advantage.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Roman society was fundamentally built on the patron-client system, as it provided the social glue that connected all levels of the hierarchy. At every level, from the poorest freedman to the emperor himself, Romans were bound by networks of mutual obligation. A senator's power depended on the number of clients who supported him; a plebeian's survival might depend on his patron's protection and generosity. The system permeated politics (clients voted as their patron directed), economics (patrons provided loans and business opportunities) and law (patrons represented clients in court). Even the emperor was described as the ultimate patron of the Roman people, distributing grain and games to his citizen-clients. However, the patron-client system alone did not structure Roman society. Legal status created rigid boundaries: the distinction between citizen and non-citizen, free and slave, patrician and plebeian was defined by law, not patronage. The family (familia) under the paterfamilias was an independent power structure. Military service created loyalty bonds separate from patronage. Furthermore, the system had significant limitations — it created dependency rather than equality, and it could not prevent social conflict when the interests of patrons and clients diverged, as seen in the Conflict of the Orders.
